body:
I have no quarrel with most of this section. It is in agreement with
what John Zerzan writes in Future Primitive, that humans were happier as
hunter gatherers. 
(for excerpts, see http://www.geocities.com/SoHo/Lofts/2532/zerzan.html)
 
> 
> 47. Among the abnormal conditions present in modern industrial society are
> excessive density of population, isolation of man from nature, excessive
> rapidity of social change and the break-down of natural small-scale
> communities such as the extended family, the village or the tribe.

true. But I wonder if Ted would have been happy in a village or tribe.


> 
> hands. For example, a variety of noise-making devices: power mowers, radios,
> motorcycles, etc. If the use of these devices is unrestricted, people who want
> peace and quiet are frustrated by the noise. If their use is restricted,
> people who use the devices are frustrated by the regulations. But if these
> machines had never been invented there would have been no conflict and no
> frustration generated by them.)

This takes on added significance, now that we know what Ted thinks of
noisy engines/machines.

> 
> 49. For primitive societies the natural world (which usually changes only
> slowly) provided a stable framework and therefore a sense of security. In the
> modern world it is human society that dominates nature rather than the other
> way around, and modern society changes very rapidly owing to technological
> change. Thus there is no stable framework.

Incredibly true. Most people can no longer go back to the area of their
childhood, or even an area they knew 10 years ago. It will have been
plowed under by Progress.
One doesn't realize the effects of constant wrenching change until one
is an older adult. (Younger people are usually more interested in
ESCAPING the world of their childhood. And, to generalize, younger
people often LOVE change & progress. Only later do they realize what
they've sacrificed in exchange.) 

> separating themselves from their communities. Beyond that, a technological
> society HAS TO weaken family ties and local communities if it is to function
> efficiently. In modern society an individual's loyalty must be first to the
> system and only secondarily to a small-scale community, because if the
> internal loyalties of small-scale communities were stronger than loyalty to
> the system, such communities would pursue their own advantage at the expense
> of the system.

In my Modern European History class we learned that the Powers That Be
encouraged mass sports events in the late 1800's, as a way of getting
the emerging working class to feel things as a group and do things as a
mass/crowd.

> 53. Crowding, rapid change and the breakdown of communities have been widely
> recognized as sources of social problems. But we do not believe they are
> enough to account for the extent of the problems that are seen today.
> 
> 54. A few pre-industrial cities were very large and crowded, yet their
> inhabitants do not seem to have suffered from psychological problems to the
> same extent as modern man. In America today there still are uncrowded rural
> areas, and we find there the same problems as in urban areas, though the
> problems tend to be less acute in the rural areas. Thus crowding does not seem
> to be the decisive factor.

This is a statement that can't be documented. How does Ted know that the
inhabitants of ancient Rome didn't feel stress? I think they did. They
also suffered the same economic problems we do. Remember the 'bread &
circuses'? Remember the Roman orgies & bulimia (Rome's gift to the
world.) Social pathology isn't a new thing.
> 
> 55. On the growing edge of the American frontier during the 19th century, the
> mobility of the population probably broke down extended families and
> small-scale social groups to at least the same extent as these are broken
> down today. In fact, many nuclear families lived by choice in such isolation,
> having no neighbors within several miles, that they belonged to no community
> at all, yet they do not seem to have developed problems as a result.

Again... how does he know they didn't? I think alcoholism & murder rates
were very high. "The Wild West". And don't forget, they took out their
frustrations by killing Indians! The West/pioneer times were very
pathological if one looks past the idyllic picture painted by the
history books.

> psychological problems. In fact, 19th century American society had an
> optimistic and self-confident tone, quite unlike that of today's society.

sure. They believed in an unlimited supply of resources to exploit, and
good ol' manifest destiny.
Plus, Ted is just talking about white males here.
I have to admit that Ted's perspective, while that of a maladjusted
genius, is still that of a white male.
